questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Center of a Vertical Hyperbola Given an Equation in Expanded Form
questions.problem:
What is the center of the hyperbola 
$-10{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}+20x+36y=64?$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in the above form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-10{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}+20x+36y & =64 \\ 9{y}^{2}+36y-10{x}^{2}+20x & =64 \\ 9[{y}^{2}+4y]-10[{x}^{2}-2x] & =64 \\ 9[(y+2)^{2}-4]-10[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =64 \\ 9(y+2)^{2}-36-10(x-1)^{2}+10 & =64 \\ 9(y+2)^{2}-10(x-1)^{2} & =64+36-10 \\ 9(y+2)^{2}-10(x-1)^{2} & =90 \\ \frac{(y+2)^{2}}{10}-\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{9} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the center is $(1,-2).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Center of a Horizontal Hyperbola Given an Equation in Expanded Form
questions.problem:
What is the center of the hyperbola 
${x}^{2}-8{y}^{2}+6x+48y=71?$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in the above form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-8{y}^{2}+6x+48y & =71 \\ {x}^{2}+6x-8{y}^{2}+48y & =71 \\ [{x}^{2}+6x]-8[{y}^{2}-6y] & =71 \\ [(x+3)^{2}-9]-8[(y-3)^{2}-9] & =71 \\ (x+3)^{2}-9-8(y-3)^{2}+72 & =71 \\ (x+3)^{2}-8(y-3)^{2} & =8 \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{8}-(y-3)^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-(-3))^{2}}{(\sqrt{8})^{2}}-\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the center is $(-3,3).$

The equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Note that the given equation can be rewritten as follows:

$$
\frac{(y-(-3))^{2}}{{5}^{2}}-\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

In this case, we have $h=4$ and $k=-3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Center of a Horizontal Hyperbola Given an Equation in Expanded Form
questions.problem:
The center of the hyperbola $4{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-8x+2y=7$ is$\,\,($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}
$).$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the given equation in standard form, group the $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-8x+2y & =7 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2x)-({y}^{2}-2y) & =7 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-1]-[(y-1)^{2}-1] & =7 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4-(y-1)^{2}+1 & =7 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-(y-1)^{2} & =7+4-1 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-(y-1)^{2} & =10 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{5/2}-\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{10} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the center of the hyperbola is $(\,1,1\,).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Center of a Vertical Hyperbola Given an Equation in Expanded Form
questions.problem:
The center of the hyperbola ${y}^{2}-4{x}^{2}-6y+8x=-1$ is$\,\,($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}
$).$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in the above form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4{x}^{2}-6y+8x & =-1 \\ {y}^{2}-6y-4{x}^{2}+8x & =-1 \\ [{y}^{2}-6y]-4[{x}^{2}-2x] & =-1 \\ [(y-3)^{2}-9]-4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =-1 \\ (y-3)^{2}-9-4(x-1)^{2}+4 & =-1 \\ (y-3)^{2}-4(x-1)^{2} & =-1+9-4 \\ (y-3)^{2}-4(x-1)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{(y-3)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}-\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the center of the hyperbola is $(\,1,3\,).$
